title: Regional policy gateways sketch and enforcement placement
content:
Purpose
This is a working sketch for where to place policy enforcement and authorization hooks across regional routing topology. Goal is to propose a pragmatic hybrid: local regional gateways (PEPs) for fast deny/fail-open semantics, backed by a central/regionally replicated PDP for policy decisions and audit. Notes are intentionally rough — design tradeoffs, failure modes, rollout checklist and open questions included.

Context / constraints
- Multi-region deployment across NA/EU/APAC with cross-region failover for latency and availability.
- Customers expect predictable latency SLOs (tail p95/p99) and strict data access controls for some tenants.
- We operate a control plane (central) and a thin regional data/control plane for routing.
- Need to support both RBAC (role-based) and ABAC (attribute based) policies depending on product feature.
- Avoid adding >5ms median token latency for hosted API call path.

Summary recommendation (short)
- Introduce a lightweight regional policy gateway (RPG) sitting at the regional edge (ingress) as the primary PEP (policy enforcement point). RPG performs fast checks for common allow/deny rules using a local policy cache and issuer-signed tokens.
- Centralized PDP (policy decision point) lives in the control plane, but is asynchronously replicated to region-local PDP instances for heavier-weight attribute evaluation and policy updates.
- Sidecar/mesh-level enforcement only for intra-cluster service-to-service policies (tenant isolation, admin actions).
- Fallback rules: if RPG can't reach local PDP, apply cached decision or configurable fail-open/fail-closed per customer SLA. Audit logs stream to central logging with region tags.

Why this hybrid?
- Pure central PDP increases RTT and adds tail risk for policy checks, harming p99 latency.
- Fully-distributed policy authoring is operationally complex and risks inconsistent enforcement on policy rollouts.
- Regional cached PDP reduces latency while keeping a single control-plane source-of-truth for policy authoring and audit.

Components and responsibilities
- Regional Policy Gateway (RPG) — PEP:
  - Location: ingress gateway (regional edge), immediately before routing to model-serving clusters.
  - Duties: parse request identity, verify token signatures, consult local policy cache for quick allow/deny, forward enriched identity headers downstream, emit audit event for every evaluated rule.
  - Fast-path: static RBAC decisions and common ABAC predicates (tenant id == resource tenant, request origin region constraint). Fast path in-memory TTL cache (small LRU) with explicit invalidation hook.
  - Slow-path: when no cache entry or complex attribute expression, call local PDP instance (sync) with <50ms budget; if no response, apply configured fallback.

- Policy Decision Point (PDP) — regional instance: 
  - Location: region-local control plane service; authoritative source is central control plane which pushes policy bundles.
  - Duties: evaluate full ABAC expressions, attribute enrichment (look up dataset tags, customer config), produce signed decision tokens (short lived).
  - Mutability: receive policy bundles and policy-version metadata from central control plane; support atomic swap and health-check before serving.

- Central Policy Service (control plane) — policy authoring and distribution: 
  - Location: central control plane, multi-AZ.
  - Duties: UI/API for policy authoring, policy history, audit, push to regional PDPs; run offline evaluations, rollout canary.

- Service mesh sidecars / intra-cluster PEPs: 
  - Use-case: internal enforcement for fine-grained microservice access (admin APIs, telemetry access).
  - Not intended for initial tenant-facing request authz due to extra hop/latency.

Decision flow (happy path)
1) Client -> Regional ingress -> RPG receives request and parsed identity (mTLS or signed bearer).
2) RPG checks token signature and extracts attributes (subject, roles, tenant, origin).
3) RPG checks in-memory policy cache for matching rule. If hit and allow/deny found, apply and emit audit.
4) If cache miss or attribute needed, RPG calls region-local PDP with attribute bag. PDP returns decision + signed token. RPG enforces and forwards request with decision header.
5) Regional logging pipelines stream audit events to central observability with region tag and policy-version.

Failure modes and recommended defaults
- PDP unavailable: RPG uses cache if present; if not, apply per-tenant fallback (default: fail-open for non-sensitive tenants, fail-closed for regulated tenants). Document fallback in customer contract.
- Policy drift during rollout: serve both old and new policy for a window; include a "policy-version" header in decisions; monitor deny-rate changes.
- Stale attributes: attribute TTL and revocation mechanism for immediate critical revokes (e.g., manual admin revoke) — push revocation to RPG via invalidation channel.

Performance considerations
- Cache hit-target: aim for >90% RPG cache hit for common request types to keep extra latency <2–5ms.
- PDP sync budget: regional PDP must answer within 50–100ms for slow-path; tune based on p95 additions to overall path.
- Signed decision token length and signing algorithm: use compact JWT-like signed blob with algorithm that verifies in <1ms at RPG.

Security & trust model
- Use mTLS and short-lived signed tokens between RPG <-> PDP <-> control plane.
- All policy bundles signed by central control plane keys; RPG and regional PDP verify signature before applying.
- Audit immutability: stream raw evaluation inputs and decisions to central immutable log (append-only) for post-hoc review.

Policy language and model
- Support a hybrid policy language: simple RBAC predicates for role checks; expression language for ABAC (attributes, time-of-day, resource labels).
- Policies authored centrally with tags: "sensitive", "latency-critical", "global" — control propagation and invalidation semantics accordingly.

Rollout plan (practical)
1) Build RPG prototype in one non-production region that mirrors production routing.
2) Implement local PDP with a minimal ABAC evaluator and signed decisions.
3) Start with allow-list RBAC for admin APIs (low-volume). Measure latency and cache hit behavior.
4) Expand to tenant-level routing; enable per-tenant fallback config.
5) Canary policies with 1–5% traffic per change; add canary harm metrics (unexpected deny, latency spike).
6) Add revocation/invalidation channel and test fail-open/fail-closed configs in chaos test.

Open questions / TODOs
- Do we need per-tenant policy sharding to prevent noisy policy updates from affecting other tenants? (performance vs complexity)
- How to express cross-region routing constraints elegantly in policy language (e.g., data residency + failover permissive rules)?
- Cost of signed decision tokens: choose compact binary vs JWT for auditability tradeoffs.
- Integration with SSO / customer identity provider attributes—pull vs push model for ABAC attributes.

Links / references
- JIRA-PLAT-421 (policy gateway prototype)
- confluence://platform/routing-policy-gateway-design (authoring guide)
- slack thread: C01ABCDEF thread-plat-routing-2024-10-29

Notes to reviewer
- This doc is a sketch: looking for feedback on fallback defaults, cache invalidation approach, and per-tenant vs global policy push model. Prefer small, testable iteration: RPG prototype -> admin APIs -> tenant APIs.
